title: Effectiveness and Safety of Selective IL-23 Receptor Antagonists in Moderate to Severe Ulcerative Colitis: A Systematic Review, Meta-Analysis and Trial Sequential Analysis
extended_summary:
This paper asks whether selective IL-23 receptor antagonists are effective and safe for treating moderate to severe ulcerative colitis, and whether the evidence base is sufficiently large and robust to support firm conclusions. The authors note that although individual randomized trials had shown promise, the overall comparative effectiveness, safety profile, and consistency across agents remained unclear.

To address this, they conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials comparing IL-23 receptor antagonists with placebo in moderate to severe ulcerative colitis. The included drugs were ustekinumab, mirikizumab, guselkumab, and risankizumab. Outcomes included clinical remission, clinical response, endoscopic remission/response, histologic and mucosal healing, symptomatic remission, quality-of-life change, and adverse events. They also conducted subgroup analyses, meta-regression, and trial sequential analysis.

The synthesis included nine RCTs representing 3,808 patients in induction and 1,734 patients in maintenance. Across both phases, IL-23 receptor antagonists improved clinical and endoscopic outcomes versus placebo and did not meaningfully worsen overall safety; serious adverse events were lower in induction and comparable in maintenance. Trial sequential analysis suggested the evidence was sufficiently powered for the main clinical outcomes. The authors conclude that IL-23 receptor antagonists are a promising and relatively safe option for moderate to severe ulcerative colitis.
quality_tier_rationale: This paper is a systematic review/meta-analysis, but it is about IL-23 receptor antagonists for ulcerative colitis, not education or AI/technology intervention in learning. It does not provide relevant evidence for the requested education taxonomy.
impact_tier_rationale: There is no educational intervention or student outcome evaluated, so it has no direct impact on K-12 learning or implementation contexts.
